plans.title: Bangladesh tea: a vermicompost transition
plans.subtitle: Helping tea-garden farmers move from synthetic fertilizer to on-garden vermicompost
plans.summary: Bangladesh's tea belt runs through the hills of Sylhet, Moulvibazar, Habiganj and Chattogram. Decades of synthetic-fertilizer use have acidified and depleted many tea soils. This plan maps the real, named tea gardens and the national research body (BTRI), and lays out a phased switch to vermicompost — worm-composted garden bio-waste and cow dung — grounded in field trials from Bangladesh (Luskerpore Tea Estate) and the wider region. It is honest about the cost: organic conversion in tea typically dips yield for the first transition years before soil biology and output recover.

entities.name: Malnicherra Tea Estate
entities.note: Oldest tea estate in the subcontinent — planted 1854.

entities.name: Bangladesh Tea Research Institute (BTRI)
entities.note: National tea R&D body; its Soil Science Division runs vermicompost and organic-input trials on mature tea.

entities.name: Luskerpore Tea Estate — vermicompost trial site
entities.note: Site of vermicompost field trials in Bangladeshi tea; a cow-dung + kitchen-residue + Eisenia foetida mix gave the best results in published work.

companies.name: National Tea Company Ltd (NTCL)
companies.facts: ≈12 A-class estates across Sylhet, ≈10,000 ha, ≈5.2 million kg/yr.

companies.name: M. M. Ispahani Ltd
companies.facts: 4 estates (Mirzapore, Zareen, Neptune, Ghazipore), ≈2,100 ha; ≈50% of the domestic branded-tea market.

companies.name: James Finlay successors
companies.facts: Finlay's Bangladesh estates (Habiganj & Moulvibazar) now run by The Consolidated Tea & Lands Co (Bangladesh) Ltd and Baraoora (Sylhet) Tea Co Ltd.

steps.title: 1 · Baseline soil & garden audit
steps.body: Test soil organic carbon, pH and N-P-K block by block, and map the worker villages tied to each garden. Decades of synthetic-N use have left many tea soils acidic and low in organic matter — the starting point BTRI's soil work targets.

steps.title: 2 · Set up on-garden vermicompost units
steps.body: Culture earthworms (Eisenia foetida) on the garden's own bio-waste — prunings and factory residue — plus cow dung. In Bangladeshi trials at Luskerpore Tea Estate (Habiganj), a cow-dung + kitchen-residue + Eisenia foetida mix gave the highest-performing vermicompost.

steps.title: 3 · Phase in vermicompost, phase down synthetic N
steps.body: Substitute incrementally — e.g. start on a quarter of blocks. Be honest about the cost: organic-conversion research in tea reports a transition-period yield dip (often up to ~20% in the first conversion years) before soil biology and yield recover. Plan cash-flow and worker income around that dip.

steps.title: 4 · Rebuild soil biology & carbon
steps.body: Vermicompost raises soil organic carbon, available nitrogen and microbial biomass. Field tea trials (e.g. vermicompost at 10 t/ha with jeevamrit) showed higher available N and microbial biomass carbon alongside improved growth and yield.

steps.title: 5 · Capture a quality / organic premium
steps.body: Organically grown tea tends to score higher on leaf-quality indicators, which can offset lower volume. A certification pathway lets converted gardens reach premium and export buyers.

steps.title: 6 · Worker-cooperative economics & scale-up
steps.body: Bangladesh's gardens employ 300,000+ plantation workers, about three-quarters women. Vermicompost can be a worker-run input enterprise — keeping value and skills inside the garden community as the practice scales across estates.

dataGaps: Per-garden ownership/operator is not consistently published. Gardens here are positioned from OpenStreetMap/Wikidata; company control is shown only where a company itself discloses it.
Farm-level cost, labour and net-income effects of switching to vermicompost in Bangladeshi tea are not quantified in the public literature — shown here as a gap, not estimated.
Most estates have no boundary polygon in OSM; each point marks a real labelled feature inside the estate, not its full extent.
